title: Find All Primes
description:
Given an integer A. Find the list of all prime numbers in the range [1, A].

Problem Constraints
1 <= A <= 10^6

Input Format
Only argument A is an integer.

Output Format
Return a sorted array of prime number in the range [1, A].

Example Input
Input 1:
A = 7
Input 2:
A = 12

Example Output
Output 1:
[2, 3, 5, 7]
Output 2:
[2, 3, 5, 7, 11]

Example Explanation
For Input 1:
The prime numbers from 1 to 7 are 2, 3, 5 and 7.
For Input 2:
The prime numbers from 1 to 12 are 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11.
story: List every prime up to A. The clean way to crack it is the Sieve of Eratosthenes: mark all multiples of each prime as composite, then collect what stays unmarked.
plain: Mark 0 and 1 as non-prime, then for each i from 2, if i is prime record it and cross out all its multiples. Collecting the unmarked numbers gives the sorted prime list.
tale: Cross out every second number after 2, every third after 3, and so on. Whatever survives the crossing-out is prime.
howToThink: "All primes up to A" with A as large as 10^6 -> don't test each number alone, sieve them all at once.
Sieve of Eratosthenes: keep a boolean array, and for each prime cross out its multiples.
Whatever stays unmarked from 2 to A is prime; collect those in order.
pitfalls: Mark 0 and 1 as non-prime before you start.
Sieve array must be size `A+1` so index `A` is valid.
Cross out multiples starting from `i*i` (smaller multiples are already marked); mark index `j`, not `i`.

solutions.label: User solution — sieve with primality check
solutions.plain: For each i, test primality via sqrt trip counting, add to list if prime, and mark multiples in the boolean array.
approach: Make an array sized A+1 and mark index 0 and 1 as not prime.
For each i from 2 to A, if not already marked and isPrimeNumber(i) is true, add i to the result list.
Copy the list into an int array and return it.
solutions.story: Note: the original submission wrote primeArray[i] inside the inner loop (dead sieve line); corrected to primeArray[j].

title: Prime Sum
description:
Given an even number A (greater than 2), return two prime numbers whose sum will be equal to the given number.
If there is more than one solution possible, return the lexicographically smaller solution.
If [a, b] is one solution with a <= b, and [c,d] is another solution with c <= d, then
[a, b] < [c, d], If a < c OR a==c AND b < d.
NOTE: A solution will always exist. Read Goldbach's conjecture.

Problem Constraints
4 <= A <= 2*10^7

Input Format
First and only argument of input is an even number A.

Output Format
Return a integer array of size 2 containing primes whose sum will be equal to given number.

Example Input
Input 1:
4

Example Output
Output 1:
[2, 2]

Example Explanation
There is only 1 solution for A = 4.
story: Split an even number into two primes (Goldbach). To crack it and get the lexicographically smallest pair, scan i from the small side and return the first i where both i and A-i are prime.
plain: Handle A=4 as [2,2]. Then loop i over odd values from 3 up to A/2; the first i where both i and A-i are prime gives the smallest pair. Scanning upward guarantees lexicographic minimality.
tale: Try the smallest prime first as one half; the first time its partner (A minus it) is also prime, you have the earliest matching pair.
howToThink: "Even number as sum of two primes" is Goldbach -> pick one half, check if the other half is prime.
For the lexicographically smallest pair, scan the smaller prime `i` upward from the bottom.
First `i` where both `i` and `A-i` are prime is the answer, so a fast `isPrime` check is all you need.
pitfalls: Special-case `A == 4` -> `[2,2]`, since scanning odds from 3 misses it.
Only loop `i` up to `A/2` so you don't return the same pair reversed.
`isPrime` must treat 0 and 1 as non-prime and loop to `sqrt(n)` inclusive.

solutions.label: User solution — scan primes from small side
solutions.plain: Special-case 4, then check each odd i and its complement A-i for primality, returning the first valid pair.
approach: Loop i from 3 to A/2 stepping by 2.
If both i and A-i are prime, return {i, A-i}.
Return null otherwise (never reached by constraints).

title: Count of divisors
description:
Given an array of integers A, find and return the count of divisors of each element of the array.
NOTE: The order of the resultant array should be the same as the input array.

Problem Constraints
1 <= length of the array <= 100000
1 <= A[i] <= 10^6

Input Format
The only argument given is the integer array A.

Output Format
Return the count of divisors of each element of the array in the form of an array.

Example Input
Input 1:
A = [2, 3, 4, 5]
Input 2:
A = [8, 9, 10]

Example Output
Output 1:
[2, 2, 3, 2]
Output 2:
[4, 3, 4]

Example Explanation
Explanation 1:
The number of divisors of 2 : [1, 2], 3 : [1, 3], 4 : [1, 2, 4], 5 : [1, 5]
So the count will be [2, 2, 3, 2].
story: For each number in the array, count its divisors. To crack it fast across many queries, precompute a divisor-count sieve up to the max value, then answer each element in O(1).
plain: Build a divisor-count array with a sieve: for every d from 1 to max, add 1 to every multiple of d. Then look up the count for each A[i]. Alternatively, count divisors of each element in O(sqrt(A[i])).
tale: Every number d ticks a mark on all its multiples; at the end each slot holds how many numbers divide into it.
howToThink: Many numbers, each needs its divisor count -> precompute once instead of testing each.
Flip the loop: every `d` is a divisor of all its multiples, so add 1 to `divCount[d], divCount[2d], ...`.
After the sieve, each query is an O(1) lookup `divCount[A[i]]`.
pitfalls: Size the sieve to the max value in `A`, not to the array length.
Keep output order the same as input; just map each `A[i]` through `divCount`.
Every number counts 1 and itself, so the minimum count is 2 (except 1, which has count 1).

solutions.label: Optimal — divisor-count sieve
solutions.plain: Find max value M, run a sieve adding 1 to divCount[multiple] for every divisor d, then map each A[i] to divCount[A[i]].
approach: Find M = max value in A.
For d = 1..M, for each multiple j = d, 2d, ...: divCount[j]++.
solutions.pseudocode:
M = max(A)
for d in 1..M:
  for j = d; j<=M; j+=d: divCount[j]++
for i: res[i] = divCount[A[i]]
return res

title: Lucky Numbers
description:
A lucky number is a number that has exactly 2 distinct prime divisors.
You are given a number A, and you need to determine the count of lucky numbers between the range 1 to A (both inclusive).

Problem Constraints:
1 <= A <= 50000

Input Format:
The first and only argument is an integer A.

Output Format:
Return an integer i.e the count of lucky numbers between 1 and A, both inclusive.
story: Count numbers up to A that have exactly two different prime factors. A modified sieve lets us tally, for every number, how many distinct primes divide it.
plain: Use a sieve: keep a count array. For each prime p, walk through all its multiples and add 1 to their distinct-prime count. At the end, count how many numbers from 1 to A have a count of exactly 2.
tale: Like stamping each locker with the initials of every prime that owns a share; lucky lockers are the ones carrying exactly two distinct stamps.
howToThink: "Exactly 2 distinct prime divisors" -> you need, per number, a count of distinct primes dividing it.
Modified sieve: for each prime `i`, walk its multiples and bump their counter by 1.
At the end, count how many values from 1 to A have a counter of exactly 2.
pitfalls: A number is prime here when its count is still 0 when you reach it (`cnt[i]==0`).
Walk multiples from `i` itself so `i` gets counted too.
Count distinct primes, not total factors, so bump once per prime, never per prime power.

solutions.label: Distinct-prime-factor sieve
solutions.plain: Sieve to count distinct prime factors of every number up to A, then count those equal to 2.
approach: Create an int array cnt of size A+1 initialised to 0.
For i from 2 to A, if cnt[i] is 0 then i is prime; for every multiple j of i, increment cnt[j].
After the sieve, count how many indices from 1 to A have cnt equal to 2.
solutions.pseudocode:
cnt = int[A+1]
for i in 2..A:
  if cnt[i]==0:            # i is prime
    for j = i; j<=A; j+=i: cnt[j]++
ans = number of x in 1..A with cnt[x]==2
return ans
